stories.headline: Update: Trump Calls Iran Conflict 'Small Potatoes' as U.S. and Iran Trade Ship Strikes
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump on Sunday described the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict as 'small potatoes,' aligning himself with Vice President JD Vance's assertion that months of on-and-off military exchanges in the Middle East no longer constitute a 'war.' The comments came as the two countries continued trading strikes on maritime vessels: the U.S. confirmed hitting three Iranian oil tankers, while Iran said it targeted three U.S.-linked ships, including an unmanned American military vessel in the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran claimed to have struck using the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright, appearing on multiple Sunday news programs, said the administration remains 'open' to a nuclear agreement with Iran but acknowledged one 'may not' be reached, suggesting the alternative could be 'destroying their capabilities' to build a nuclear weapon. Wright also said U.S. Navy escorts helping tankers transit the Strait of Hormuz are 'essential' and will not end soon. OPEC and allied oil-producing nations met Sunday following the resumption of U.S.-Iran strikes, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could fall to $40-$50 per barrel once the conflict ends.

Critics, including former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall III, questioned the strategic rationale for the conflict, saying on ABC's 'This Week' that he could not understand what advice led Trump to 'start this conflict' and that he had 'never seen an attempt to politicize our military' like that of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Congressional Democrats, including Rep. Jason Crow, said Congress has not been fully briefed on related Pentagon leak investigations.

With nine outlets covering the story, the continued military exchanges and Trump's dismissive characterization of the conflict represent a significant new development in an ongoing crisis affecting global energy markets and regional stability.

stories.headline: Building Collapse in New Delhi Traps Dozens of Students
stories.summary:
A five-storey residential building collapsed Sunday afternoon in the Satya Niketan neighborhood of south-west New Delhi, with as many as 50 people — many of them university students — feared trapped inside. At least one person was killed and two others left in critical condition, according to local police cited by NDTV. Six people had been rescued as of initial reports, with some trapped students reportedly making phone calls from beneath the rubble.

The building, known as Hostel Daze and located near the Delhi University campus, was undergoing construction work in its basement at the time of the collapse. A shopkeeper nearby told news agency ANI that excavation work had been carried out to increase rental income, but that while the upper structure had been reinforced, the foundation pillars had been left weakened. Delhi Police said the building was between 40 and 50 years old.

Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated as a precautionary measure and that 'every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped.' The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate and hold those responsible to account, warning that 'negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated.' Police are searching for the building's owner.

The collapse highlights ongoing concerns about building safety enforcement in India's rapidly urbanizing cities, where unauthorized construction and inadequate structural inspections remain persistent problems.

stories.headline: Update: Witkoff and Kushner Meet Zelensky in Kyiv After Putin Talks in Moscow
stories.summary:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday, a day after holding more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. A Kremlin aide described the Moscow session as 'highly useful,' and the back-to-back visits mark the most intensive American diplomatic push yet to broker a ceasefire in the nearly six-year-old war.

The meetings represent a concrete new development in Trump's effort to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict, with both sides now having received direct engagement from the president's top envoys in the span of 24 hours. The substance of the Kyiv talks was not immediately disclosed. Senator John Kennedy (R-La.), speaking on NBC's Meet the Press, called the ongoing negotiations 'pretty talk' that likely will not end the war, and criticized Republican leadership for what he described as a missed opportunity to pass Russia sanctions.

The diplomatic sprint comes as the U.S. is simultaneously engaged in the Iran conflict, stretching American foreign policy bandwidth across two major theaters simultaneously. Zelensky's government has previously expressed skepticism about U.S. proposals that would require territorial concessions, while Moscow has insisted on security guarantees precluding Ukrainian NATO membership as a precondition for any agreement.

The Kyiv visit is the first by Witkoff and Kushner to the Ukrainian capital and follows months of shuttle diplomacy that has yet to produce a ceasefire framework. The development is covered by multiple major outlets and represents a material step forward in what has been a largely stalled peace process.

stories.headline: Odesa Considers Banning Russian Language in Public Arts and Culture
stories.summary:
City councillors in Odesa, Ukraine's third-largest city, are set to vote this week on a proposal to ban Russian-language content in music, literature, and public arts venues — including streets, parks, public institutions, and state-run entertainment spaces. The ban would extend to privately owned spaces by recommendation and would require all Russian-language books to be removed from display in public libraries. The vote is particularly notable because Odesa is an overwhelmingly Russian-speaking city, home to celebrated Russian-language writers and musicians.

Supporters of the measure argue that the Russian language has been weaponized by Moscow as a tool to undermine Ukrainian identity and influence younger generations raised in Russian-speaking environments. Odesa lawyer Artem Kartashov, who has advised local authorities on a broader 'decolonisation' programme, said: 'The Russian language is a weapon of Russia, and we need to try to fix that.'

Critics warn the ban could backfire. Comic actor Borys Barsky, one of Odesa's best-known entertainers, said Russian is not only Putin's language but the language of Dostoyevsky and Bulgakov, and that pitting Russian-speaking Ukrainians against each other serves only Putin's interests. Russian President Vladimir Putin has historically cited alleged repression of Russian speakers in Ukraine as a pretext for the invasion, a claim widely dismissed as false.

The proposal builds on existing national legislation requiring Ukrainian in many public and professional contexts, passed in 2019. The outcome of the Odesa vote could set a significant precedent for other majority Russian-speaking cities in Ukraine grappling with questions of cultural identity during the ongoing war.

stories.headline: Michigan Senate Race: GOP Targets Democrat El-Sayed Over Progressive Ties as Race Heats Up
stories.summary:
Michigan's 2026 Senate race is intensifying as Republicans focus scrutiny on Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed's past associations and policy positions, even as El-Sayed seeks to present a more moderate image to general-election voters. Since launching his campaign in April 2025, El-Sayed has publicly distanced himself from several prior left-wing positions and repeatedly insisted he is 'not a socialist,' telling CNN in July: 'I believe in capitalism, I just believe that capitalism has to be regulated.'

Republicans, including Florida Representative Kat Cammack, have focused on El-Sayed's ties to figures such as Twitch streamer Hasan Piker — who claimed America 'deserved' 9/11 — as well as endorsements from Senator Bernie Sanders and associations with individuals accused of antisemitism and socialist activism. The El-Sayed campaign acknowledged no campaign surrogate speaks for the candidate and sought to redirect attention to Republican nominee Mike Rogers, noting some Rogers-affiliated individuals have questioned the 2020 election outcome and advocated for banning gay marriage.

The Michigan Senate race is one of the most closely watched contests of the 2026 midterm cycle, with control of the Senate potentially hinging on the outcome. El-Sayed is the first Muslim-American major-party nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan's history, and the race has drawn national attention and significant outside spending.

Both sides are deploying opposition research aggressively. Democrats argue the Rogers campaign's own associations undercut Republican attacks, while Republicans contend El-Sayed's moderation is a strategic repositioning rather than a genuine shift, citing his refusal to sever ties with progressive allies.

stories.headline: Prince William to Represent King Charles at King Harald's Funeral in Norway
stories.summary:
Buckingham Palace has announced that Prince William, the Prince of Wales, will attend the state funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, representing his father King Charles III. Princess Anne will also attend in a personal capacity, as she is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII. The attendance follows the convention that reigning monarchs do not typically attend the funerals of other heads of state.

King Harald, who died last month at the age of 89, had reigned for 35 years and was widely regarded as a popular, modernising figure who helped bring the Norwegian monarchy closer to its people, including by breaking with tradition to marry a commoner. Thousands have queued to pay their respects during his lying in state at the Royal Palace chapel in Oslo.

The funeral on September 9 will include a procession through Oslo followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral and a private burial at the Akershus Fortress royal mausoleum. European royals from across the continent are expected to attend. King Charles, who is Harald's cousin, praised him for serving Norway with 'unwavering dedication' and guiding the country 'with warmth and humility.'

King Haakon VIII ascends the throne at a challenging moment for the Norwegian royal family, which has faced a series of public scandals including Queen Mette-Marit's disclosed friendship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the June rape conviction of her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is appealing.

stories.headline: Haitian TPS Workers Fired Across U.S. Healthcare Sector After Supreme Court Ruling
stories.summary:
Hundreds of thousands of Haitians who held Temporary Protected Status (TPS) lost the right to work legally in the United States at the end of July, following a Supreme Court ruling in favor of the Trump administration's decision to terminate the program. The ruling affected approximately 350,000 Haitian TPS holders and has had an immediate and tangible impact on the American healthcare and direct-care workforce, where Haitians represent one of the top five immigrant groups.

Employers across the country, particularly nonprofits and care facilities serving individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities, have been forced to terminate affected workers. Families who relied on those caregivers are now scrambling for alternatives in an industry that was already severely understaffed. 'We simply do not have enough people in our domestic market, when you exclude immigrants, to fill those jobs,' said Kezia Scales of the Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute.

The Trump administration first announced the TPS termination for Haitians in June 2025, framing it as part of a broader effort to enforce immigration law and prioritize legal pathways. More than a dozen countries have had TPS terminated during Trump's second term, with Haitians making up nearly a third of all TPS recipients affected. Immigration was a top issue for voters in the 2024 election, and both Long Island counties — where many affected families live — decisively backed Trump.

Advocacy groups are calling on Congress to establish longer-term legal pathways for international caregivers, arguing the terminations have worsened an existing staffing crisis. The administration has not announced any replacement workforce policy for the affected care sector.

stories.headline: Anak Krakatau Eruption Strands 150,000 Passengers, Closes Six Indonesian Airports
stories.summary:
A major eruption of Anak Krakatau volcano beginning late Friday has forced Indonesian authorities to suspend operations at six airports, including Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, stranding more than 150,000 passengers and canceling or disrupting 467 flights as of Sunday. Volcanic ash reached altitudes of up to 50,000 feet on the Sumatra side of the Sunda Strait and 20,000 feet over Java, spreading toward West Java and affecting international routes to Singapore, Doha, Sydney, and Kuala Lumpur.

Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi urged airlines to divert flights to alternate airports and expedite ticket refunds for affected passengers. Indonesia's health minister advised residents in affected areas to remain indoors and wear face masks to guard against respiratory, eye, and skin irritation from ash fallout. Local reports described ash accumulation thick enough to require sweeping every few minutes in some neighborhoods, and several schools canceled activities after students reported eye irritation.

Authorities confirmed there is no tsunami warning associated with the current eruption activity. Anak Krakatau, which translates as 'Child of Krakatoa,' has been sporadically active since emerging from the sea in the early 20th century. Its most recent major event was a 2018 collapse that triggered a tsunami killing more than 400 people along nearby Sumatran and Javan coastlines. The scale of the current travel disruption and the geographic reach of the ash cloud make this one of the most operationally significant volcanic events in the region in recent years.

stories.headline: Update: Trump's MAGA Inc. Super-PAC Pours $10 Million Into Texas Senate Race as Paxton-Talarico Contest Tightens
stories.summary:
President Trump's MAGA Inc. super-PAC has made its largest single expenditure of the 2026 midterm cycle, committing $10 million to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas, according to Federal Election Commission filings published Saturday. The funds were directed to political media company Del Ray Media and are being used to finance attack advertisements against Paxton's Democratic opponent, state Representative James Talarico.

The spending reflects growing Republican concern that what has historically been a safe GOP seat may be genuinely competitive this cycle. Polls consistently show Paxton and Talarico running neck and neck, an unusual dynamic for Texas statewide races. The investment marks a significant escalation in the national attention focused on the contest.

Paxton, a two-term attorney general who survived a 2021 impeachment effort by the Texas House, has faced sustained criticism over his legal record and conduct in office. Democrats view Talarico, a younger progressive state legislator, as a candidate capable of capitalizing on shifting suburban voter sentiment. The Texas race is now considered one of the premier Senate battlegrounds heading into November, with national party money flowing to both sides.

stories.headline: Gallup Data Show Democrats Holding Largest Party-Affiliation Advantage Since 2008 Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
New Gallup quarterly party affiliation data show Democrats holding their largest advantage over Republicans since 2008, with 31 percent of voters now identifying as Democrats compared to 28 percent when President Trump began his second term. Among self-identified independents, 49 percent say they lean Democratic versus 39 percent who prefer Republicans — a four-percentage-point shift toward Democrats since the first quarter of 2025 and a nine-point drop in Republican preference among independents since late 2022.

Analysts attribute the shift in part to Trump's declining approval ratings and persistent inflation, which has remained above the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target since the U.S.-Iran conflict began in February. Voters surveyed cited Middle East tensions and rising fuel and shipping costs as primary drivers of their dissatisfaction with the administration.

Republicans are contesting the trajectory by seeking to draw contrasts with progressive Democratic figures, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul el-Sayed, arguing those candidates will alienate centrist voters. The Republican National Committee is holding a midterm convention in Texas this week framing the party's message around a 'common sense versus crazy' contrast. The Gallup survey was conducted with a combined random sample of more than 3,000 U.S. adults and carries a margin of error of two percentage points.

stories.headline: Update: Survivor Pulled from Mud-Buried Home More Than Ten Days After Nepal-China Flood Disaster
stories.summary:
Rescuers in Nepal's Nuwakot district have recovered a 64-year-old woman, Chandika Shrestha, alive from the fourth floor of her partially mud-buried home more than ten days after catastrophic flooding and landslides tore through Himalayan valleys. She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, according to Reuters. The rescue extends a remarkable streak of survivor recoveries well beyond the typical window for such disasters.

The Nepal-China flood event, previously covered when the death toll reached 1,375, continues to generate search-and-rescue activity across affected districts. The discovery of Shrestha alive underscores the scale of destruction — with many buildings partially submerged under debris — and the ongoing nature of relief operations more than a week after the initial disaster. Authorities have not released an updated consolidated death toll in connection with this latest development.
